questions.text: Three investors are forming a new business and are deciding between organizing as a C corporation, an S corporation, or a partnership. They anticipate losses in the first two years followed by significant profitability. Which characteristic is UNIQUE to S corporations and restricts their use?

answers.text: S corporations are limited to 100 shareholders, may only issue one class of stock, and cannot have nonresident alien shareholders or most entity shareholders (with limited exceptions)
S corporations are subject to double taxation at both the entity and shareholder level — the same as C corporations
S corporations must use a fiscal year ending June 30 and cannot change their tax year once elected
S corporations are required to have at least three shareholders to maintain their pass-through status

explanations.a: S corporation eligibility requirements under §1361: (1) Maximum 100 shareholders (certain family members count as one shareholder); (2) Only one class of stock permitted — voting vs. nonvoting stock of the same economic terms is permitted, but different economic rights (different dividend or liquidation rights) are not; (3) Shareholders must be US citizens or resident aliens — nonresident alien shareholders are prohibited; (4) Shareholders must generally be individuals, certain trusts, or estates — partnerships, C corporations, and most LLCs cannot be shareholders. These restrictions make S corporations unsuitable for complex ownership structures, foreign investors, or businesses expecting rapid growth through multiple equity classes (venture capital often requires preferred stock with different economic rights).
explanations.b: S corporations are pass-through entities — income passes through to shareholders and is taxed only at the individual level (with some exceptions such as built-in gains tax). This distinguishes them from C corporations, which are subject to double taxation (entity-level corporate tax on income, then shareholder-level tax on dividends).
explanations.c: S corporations generally must use a calendar year unless they can establish a business purpose for a fiscal year or make a §444 election for a limited deferral year. There is no June 30 requirement, and the tax year is not permanently fixed — changes can be requested.
explanations.d: There is no minimum shareholder requirement for S corporations. A one-person S corporation (a single shareholder-employee) is a common and fully permissible structure. The maximum is 100 shareholders, but there is no minimum above one.

questions.text: A startup technology company expects losses of $500,000 over its first three years and then rapid profitability and a potential acquisition exit within 5-7 years. The founders anticipate needing multiple rounds of venture capital financing (preferred stock). Which entity structure is MOST tax-advantageous for these specific circumstances?

answers.text: S corporation — pass-through losses flow directly to founders in the early years when they can use them, and the single-class-of-stock restriction can be accommodated with careful structuring

C corporation — despite double taxation on ultimate exit, C corporations accommodate multiple classes of stock required by VC investors (preferred stock), Section 1202 QSBS may eliminate capital gains on exit, and losses can be preserved at the entity level for future high-rate offset

Partnership (or LLC taxed as partnership) — maximum flexibility in allocations, no shareholder restrictions, can issue equity interests with varying economic rights, and losses flow through to partners
Sole proprietorship — provides the simplest structure and maximizes loss utilization for the founding individual

explanations.a: The S corporation's single-class-of-stock restriction is a fundamental barrier to venture capital investment. VC investors uniformly require preferred stock with liquidation preferences, anti-dilution rights, and preferential returns — all of which constitute a second class of stock that disqualifies S election. S corporations are generally incompatible with VC-backed startups.
explanations.b: C corporation analysis for VC-backed tech startup: (1) Multiple equity classes: C corporations can issue preferred stock with any economic terms — essential for VC investment (liquidation preferences, participating preferred, anti-dilution); (2) §1202 Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS): shareholders of a qualified C corporation may exclude up to $10 million (or 10× basis) of gain from sale of QSBS held more than 5 years — potentially eliminating capital gains tax entirely on the exit; this is a powerful tax benefit that tips the analysis strongly toward C corporation for VC-backed startups; (3) Early losses: while losses don't flow through to shareholders (a disadvantage), the corporation can accumulate NOL carryforwards; (4) Employee options: ISOs are available in C corporations — favorable tax treatment for employee equity; (5) The combination of QSBS exclusion + VC compatibility typically outweighs the double-taxation concern for high-growth startups.
explanations.c: While partnerships/LLCs are highly flexible, VC investors and institutional investors often strongly prefer (or require) C corporation structure for investment. Many VC funds are prohibited from investing in pass-through entities due to UBTI concerns for their tax-exempt limited partners. Additionally, employees prefer C corporation stock options (ISOs) with favorable tax treatment, which are unavailable in partnerships.
explanations.d: A sole proprietorship cannot have multiple owners (founders plural), issue equity to investors, or provide limited liability protection. It is fundamentally incompatible with the multi-founder, VC-funded startup structure described.

questions.text: Two equal partners are considering liquidating their partnership. The partnership has $400,000 of cash, land (basis $50,000, FMV $180,000), and inventory (basis $30,000, FMV $70,000). Each partner has an outside basis of $120,000. Analyze the tax consequences to the partners on a liquidating distribution of the land and inventory (assume cash is retained for other purposes).

answers.text: Each partner recognizes no gain or loss on the liquidating distribution; each partner's basis in the land = $60,000 and basis in inventory = $60,000
The partnership recognizes $170,000 of gain on distribution of appreciated assets ($180,000 − $50,000 land gain + $70,000 − $30,000 inventory gain) taxed at the entity level
Each partner recognizes no gain; each partner's basis in the land received = $90,000 and basis in inventory = $30,000 (carryover from partnership), with outside basis reduced to $0
Each partner receives land worth $90,000 and inventory worth $35,000; each recognizes gain equal to the difference between FMV received and their outside basis

explanations.a: The basis allocation in a liquidating distribution is not based on outside basis divided equally among distributed assets. The §732(b) substituted basis rule applies differently — the total outside basis is allocated to received property based on specific rules.
explanations.b: Partnerships do not recognize gain on distributing appreciated property in liquidating distributions — unlike C corporations (§336). This is a fundamental difference: partnerships can distribute appreciated property tax-free (to the entity), while C corporations must recognize gain on appreciated property distributions.
explanations.c: Liquidating partnership distribution analysis (assuming equal in-kind distribution): Each partner receives 50% of each asset. Per-partner amounts: Land: basis $25,000, FMV $90,000; Inventory: basis $15,000, FMV $35,000. Each partner's outside basis = $120,000. Under §732(b), in a liquidating distribution, the basis of distributed property is determined by the partner's outside basis reduced by cash received ($0 here). Total property received by each partner has partnership basis of $25,000 + $15,000 = $40,000. The partner's outside basis ($120,000) exceeds the partnership's aggregate basis in distributed assets ($40,000). Under §732(c): basis is first assigned to each asset based on their partnership bases ($25,000 land, $15,000 inventory), then excess outside basis ($120,000 − $40,000 = $80,000) is allocated to the appreciated assets (land) based on FMV ratios. Land FMV $90,000 vs. inventory FMV $35,000 = 72%/28% split. Land gets additional basis of $80,000 × 72% ≈ $57,600; inventory gets $80,000 × 28% ≈ $22,400. Simplified: land basis ≈ $25,000 + $57,600 = $82,600; inventory basis ≈ $15,000 + $22,400 = $37,400. Option B's $90,000 land basis and $30,000 inventory basis represents an approximation of the full allocation. The key point: no gain/loss recognized on the liquidating distribution of only property.
explanations.d: In a liquidating distribution of only property (no cash), gain is recognized only if money received exceeds outside basis — not applicable here. The comparison of FMV to outside basis does not trigger gain in a property-only liquidating distribution.

questions.text: A CPA advising a client on entity selection prepares a comparison of forming either a C corporation or an S corporation to operate a profitable consulting business. The client expects $300,000 of annual net income, will need to pay a reasonable $120,000 salary, and intends to distribute all remaining profits. The client is in the 37% individual tax bracket. Analyze the comparative total tax cost under each structure for the $300,000 of annual net income.

answers.text: C corporation: total tax = $63,000 (21% entity tax only); S corporation: total tax = $111,000 (37% individual rate on all income)
C corporation: total tax = $83,160 (entity tax $63,000 + individual tax on dividends $20,160); S corporation: total tax = $111,000 (37% on all pass-through income); C corporation has lower total tax
Both structures produce identical total tax because pass-through and double taxation always equilibrate at the same effective rate

C corporation: total tax ≈ $78,300 (21% on $300,000 = $63,000 entity + 20% LTCG on $237,000 remaining after entity tax = $15,300 approximate individual tax on qualified dividends); S corporation: total tax ≈ $66,600 (37% on $180,000 pass-through + FICA savings on $120,000 salary vs. full self-employment); S corporation results in lower total tax in this scenario

explanations.a: This calculation incorrectly applies the 37% rate to the entire S corporation pass-through without considering that the $120,000 salary is already included in income and subject to both income and payroll taxes. Additionally, dividends from C corporations are taxed at qualified dividend rates (0/15/20%), not ordinary income rates — the C corporation total tax is understated.
explanations.b: The C corporation analysis uses a 15% dividend rate but misses the proper calculation. At the client's income level, qualified dividends are taxed at 20% (plus 3.8% NIIT). More importantly, the S corporation analysis fails to account for the FICA/self-employment tax savings.
explanations.c: C and S corporations produce different total tax outcomes for high-income taxpayers. The double taxation of C corporations (21% corporate + 20% dividend rate on distributed earnings) generally exceeds S corporation single-level taxation at the individual rate, particularly for taxpayers who distribute all profits annually.
explanations.d: Comparative analysis: C Corporation: Entity taxable income = $300,000 − $120,000 salary = $180,000. Corporate tax = $180,000 × 21% = $37,800. After-tax corporate income = $142,200 available for dividend. Individual tax on salary = $120,000 × 37% = $44,400 (+ FICA employer/employee). Dividend tax = $142,200 × 20% (qualified dividend rate at this income level, approximately) = $28,440. Plus 3.8% NIIT: $142,200 × 3.8% = $5,404. C corp total approximate tax (ignoring FICA): $37,800 + $44,400 + $28,440 + $5,404 ≈ $116,044. S Corporation: Pass-through income = $180,000 ($300,000 − $120,000 salary). Individual tax on pass-through = $180,000 × 37% = $66,600. Individual tax on salary = $120,000 × 37% = $44,400. FICA on salary saves vs. SE tax on full $300,000. S corp total approximate (ignoring FICA): $66,600 + $44,400 = $111,000. The S corporation results in lower total individual tax in most cases at high income levels because qualified dividend rates plus corporate tax exceed individual pass-through rates for high-bracket taxpayers.

questions.text: A C corporation expects taxable income of $500,000 in the current year and has $300,000 of NOL carryforwards from prior years (all post-2017). The corporation wants to minimize its current-year federal income tax. What is the maximum NOL deduction the corporation may claim?

answers.text: $400,000 — the corporation may deduct 80% of the $500,000 taxable income, which is more than the available $300,000 NOL carryforward, so the full $300,000 is deductible
$300,000 — the corporation can deduct the full NOL carryforward in a single year

$240,000 — the 80% limitation on taxable income ($500,000 × 80% = $400,000) exceeds the available carryforward ($300,000), so the entire $300,000 carryforward is usable; wait — the 80% cap is $400,000 and the carryforward is $300,000, so the full $300,000 is deductible
$0 — C corporations may not carry NOLs forward under current law; they can only carry them back

explanations.a: Post-2017 NOL deduction analysis: (1) 80% limitation = $500,000 taxable income × 80% = $400,000 maximum NOL deduction; (2) Available NOL carryforward = $300,000; (3) Actual NOL deduction = min($400,000 limitation, $300,000 available) = $300,000; (4) Taxable income after NOL deduction = $500,000 − $300,000 = $200,000; (5) Federal tax = $200,000 × 21% = $42,000. The full $300,000 NOL is usable because the 80% cap ($400,000) exceeds the available carryforward. No NOL remains for future years. If the NOL had been $600,000, only $400,000 could be used in the current year (80% of $500,000), with $200,000 carried forward to subsequent years.
explanations.b: While using the full $300,000 NOL produces the correct answer, the reasoning omits the 80% limitation analysis. The statement that a corporation can always deduct the full NOL ignores the TCJA's 80% limitation that caps the NOL deduction at 80% of current taxable income — though in this case, the cap ($400,000) exceeds the available NOL ($300,000), so the full $300,000 is deductible.
explanations.c: The reasoning in option C correctly walks through the analysis and reaches the right conclusion ($300,000 deductible), but the answer choice structure is confusingly written. Option B states the same conclusion more clearly.
explanations.d: Post-2017 NOLs carry forward indefinitely — they do not expire and cannot generally be carried back (with limited exceptions for farming losses). The elimination of the carryback applies to post-2017 NOLs; the carryforward was simultaneously made indefinite.

questions.text: A multistate C corporation operates in three states. State A uses a three-factor apportionment formula (payroll, property, sales — equally weighted). The corporation has the following data: total payroll $4,000,000 (State A $800,000); total property $10,000,000 (State A $2,000,000); total sales $20,000,000 (State A $6,000,000). Calculate the apportionment percentage for State A.

answers.text: 30% — apportionment = average of payroll (20%), property (20%), and sales (30%) factors
30% — the sales factor alone determines State A's apportionment because destination-based sales always govern
20% — apportionment uses only the property and payroll factors because sales are not a reliable measure of nexus

explanations.a: Option A states 30% without showing the calculation. The correct average of the three equal-weight factors (20%, 20%, 30%) is 23.33%, not 30%.
explanations.b: Three-factor equal-weighted apportionment calculation: (1) Payroll factor = State A payroll / Total payroll = $800,000 / $4,000,000 = 20.0%; (2) Property factor = State A property / Total property = $2,000,000 / $10,000,000 = 20.0%; (3) Sales factor = State A sales / Total sales = $6,000,000 / $20,000,000 = 30.0%; (4) Apportionment percentage = (20.0% + 20.0% + 30.0%) / 3 = 70.0% / 3 = 23.33%. Note: Many states have moved away from the three-factor equal-weighted formula toward a single-sales-factor or double-weighted sales formula. Tax planning implications: corporations can reduce state tax burden by locating payroll and property outside high-tax states while maintaining sales relationships there — sales factor is often less controllable than property/payroll factors.
explanations.c: Single-sales-factor apportionment is used by some states (California, Illinois, for example), but the question specifies a three-factor formula with equal weights. The sales factor alone (30%) would apply only in a single-factor state.
explanations.d: Sales are a recognized and common apportionment factor. All three factors (payroll, property, sales) are used in the classic Massachusetts-formula three-factor approach. Sales represent the market-based connection between the corporation and the state.

questions.text: A C corporation's tax advisor recommends accelerating depreciation deductions into the current year and deferring recognition of a $200,000 service revenue contract to next year. The corporation is currently in the 21% bracket and expects to remain at 21% next year. Congress is not expected to change tax rates. What is the tax benefit of this timing strategy?

answers.text: No benefit — when tax rates are constant, the timing of income and deductions has no effect on total taxes paid over both years
Significant benefit — accelerating deductions and deferring income generates a tax refund in Year 1 that is larger than the tax owed in Year 2

Time value of money benefit — deferring $200,000 of income to Year 2 and accelerating deductions to Year 1 reduces Year 1 tax, providing use of the tax savings for one additional year before the tax is due in Year 2
No benefit — tax authorities require matching income and deductions within the same year under the all-events test

explanations.a: When tax rates are constant across periods, the TOTAL taxes paid over the multi-year period are the same regardless of timing. However, the TIME VALUE of money creates a real benefit — paying tax one year later is worth the opportunity cost of those funds. This is not zero benefit; it is a timing benefit with a present-value impact.
explanations.b: There is no refund generated — the accelerated deductions reduce Year 1 tax, and the deferred income increases Year 2 tax by a similar amount (at the same rate). The cash flow benefit is that the tax savings in Year 1 can be invested for one year before the corresponding tax on the deferred income is due in Year 2.
explanations.c: Tax benefit from timing strategy at constant rates: (1) Defer $200,000 of service revenue to Year 2: reduces Year 1 tax by $200,000 × 21% = $42,000; increases Year 2 tax by $42,000; (2) Accelerate depreciation to Year 1: reduces Year 1 tax by the accelerated depreciation amount × 21%; shifts tax from Year 1 to Year 2 (or beyond, depending on depreciation method); (3) Net effect at constant rates: the total tax over both years is identical — but the corporation has use of the $42,000 (deferred service income tax savings) for one additional year. At a 5% investment return, the one-year time value of $42,000 = $42,000 × 5% = $2,100 of economic benefit. This compounding time value is the economic rationale for tax deferral strategies even when rates are constant.
explanations.d: The all-events test under the accrual method determines when income and deductions are recognized — it establishes the timing of recognition under generally accepted accounting and tax principles. It does not prevent tax planning strategies that legitimately defer income (e.g., using the completed-contract method where available, or timing service delivery) or accelerate deductions (bonus depreciation, §179).

questions.text: A C corporation had $800,000 taxable income last year. This year it expects a $350,000 net operating loss due to a major equipment write-down and business downturn. It has made $40,000 in estimated tax payments this year. Its prior-year tax was $168,000 (21% × $800,000). What estimated tax payment strategy minimizes the risk of underpayment penalties while preserving cash flow?

answers.text: Make no additional payments — the $40,000 already paid is sufficient because the corporation expects a loss and will owe no additional tax
Pay 100% of prior-year tax ($168,000 total) in equal quarterly installments, reducing additional payments to $128,000 for the year
File for an automatic extension, which waives all estimated tax payment requirements for the extension period

Use the annualized income installment method — estimate taxable income for each quarter and pay 25% of the annualized quarterly amount; this method prevents overpaying estimated taxes in early quarters when income is uncertain, avoiding both penalty and unnecessary cash outlays

explanations.a: The $40,000 already paid may be insufficient to cover estimated tax obligations for the prior-year safe harbor requirement. Prior-year tax was $168,000, so 100% of prior-year tax = $168,000; $40,000 leaves $128,000 still needed for safe harbor. Additionally, if actual income this year is not a loss but remains positive (income projections can be wrong), the corporation would face a large underpayment penalty.
explanations.b: Paying $168,000 total (prior-year safe harbor) eliminates penalty risk but commits the corporation to $128,000 of additional payments even if the actual current-year tax will be $0 (or a refund). This preserves the safe harbor but sacrifices cash flow unnecessarily when a loss is expected.
explanations.c: Filing an extension extends the time to file the tax return — it does NOT waive or extend estimated tax payment obligations for corporations. Estimated taxes are due on the original quarterly due dates (April 15, June 15, September 15, December 15 for calendar-year C corporations) regardless of any filing extension.
explanations.d: The annualized income installment method under §6655(e)(2) allows corporations to base each quarterly estimated payment on actual year-to-date income annualized to the full year: (1) Q1 payment based on annualized Q1 income; (2) Q2 payment based on annualized Q1-Q2 income; etc. If income is low or negative in early quarters (due to the equipment write-down timing), early-quarter payments are reduced or eliminated; (3) This method prevents both overpayment (tying up cash in excessive estimated taxes) and underpayment penalties (each quarterly payment matches actual income trends); (4) For a corporation expecting a loss, annualized installment method will result in minimal or zero estimated payments in loss quarters — far better than paying the full $168,000 prior-year safe harbor; (5) This is the optimal balance between penalty avoidance and cash flow preservation.

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: C corporation shareholder planning — proposed transaction implications for both entity and shareholder (noncash contributions and distributions)
questions.text: A sole shareholder is considering contributing appreciated property (basis $40,000, FMV $150,000) to her wholly owned C corporation in exchange for additional stock. She will own 100% of the corporation before and after the contribution. What are the immediate tax consequences of this §351 exchange?

answers.text: Neither the shareholder nor the corporation recognizes gain; the shareholder's stock basis increases by $40,000 (her carryover basis in the contributed property); the corporation's basis in the property is $40,000
The shareholder recognizes a $110,000 taxable gain because the contribution to a corporation is treated as a taxable sale at fair market value
The corporation recognizes $110,000 of gain and pays corporate tax on the built-in appreciation upon receipt of the property
The shareholder recognizes $110,000 of long-term capital gain, and the corporation receives a stepped-up basis of $150,000 in the property

explanations.a: §351 exchange consequences: (1) Shareholder: no gain recognized (§351(a)); new stock basis = adjusted basis of contributed property = $40,000 (§358 substituted basis); the $110,000 of unrealized gain is preserved in the reduced stock basis; (2) Corporation: no gain recognized upon receipt of property (§1032); basis in the property = contributing shareholder's basis = $40,000 (§362 carryover basis); the corporation inherits the built-in gain — if it later sells the property for $150,000, it will recognize the $110,000 gain. The §351 exchange defers, but does not eliminate, the built-in gain. If the shareholder withdraws the property through liquidation or distribution, double taxation (corporate gain + shareholder dividend/capital gain) may result — an important planning consideration.
explanations.b: Section 351 provides nonrecognition treatment for property contributions to a corporation when the contributing shareholders control (≥80%) the corporation immediately after the exchange. As the 100% shareholder before and after, §351 applies — no gain or loss is recognized.
explanations.c: The corporation does not recognize gain on receipt of property in exchange for its own stock (§1032). The corporation's obligation runs to future gain recognition when it later sells the property — not at the time of contribution.
explanations.d: Both gain recognition and stepped-up basis in the corporation would apply in a taxable sale transaction — not in a §351 exchange. The entire purpose of §351 is to defer recognition and maintain the carryover basis chain.

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: C corporation shareholder planning — proposed transaction implications for both entity and shareholder (noncash contributions and distributions)
questions.text: A C corporation shareholder is considering two alternative ways to receive funds from the corporation: (A) salary of $100,000, or (B) dividend of $100,000. The corporation is in the 21% tax bracket and the shareholder is in the 37% ordinary income and 20% long-term capital gain/qualified dividend brackets. Compare the total combined tax cost (corporation + shareholder) for each alternative.

answers.text: Both alternatives produce identical total tax because the IRS requires reasonable compensation to equalize the tax treatment of salary and dividends

Salary: corporation deducts $100,000 saving $21,000 in corporate tax; shareholder pays $37,000 income tax + FICA; Dividend: corporation pays $21,000 corporate tax on income; shareholder pays $20,000 dividend tax; total tax on salary = approximately $55,800 (after FICA); total tax on dividend = $41,000

Salary: total tax (corporate + shareholder) ≈ $55,800 (no corporate tax on deducted salary + $37,000 income tax + FICA); Dividend: total tax ≈ $41,000 ($21,000 corporate tax + $20,000 qualified dividend tax); dividends are more tax-efficient at high brackets despite double taxation
Dividends always produce lower total tax than salary in a C corporation context because corporate rates are lower than individual rates

explanations.a: The IRS does require reasonable compensation (preventing excessive salary to avoid dividends in closely held corporations), but this is a maximum reasonableness standard for salary — it does not equalize total tax. The two methods produce demonstrably different combined tax burdens.
explanations.b: Detailed comparison: Alternative A — Salary of $100,000: Corporation deducts salary: $100,000 × 21% = $21,000 corporate tax savings (net corporate tax on this income = $0 after deduction). Shareholder pays income tax: $100,000 × 37% = $37,000. FICA: employee portion $100,000 × 7.65% = $7,650; employer portion $100,000 × 7.65% = $7,650 (additional corporate cost, deductible). Total tax: $37,000 individual + $7,650 employee FICA + $7,650 employer FICA = approximately $52,300 (plus minor details). Alternative B — Dividend of $100,000: Corporation earns $100,000 and pays corporate tax: $100,000 × 21% = $21,000. After-tax amount available = $79,000 (but to deliver $100,000 to shareholder, corp needs pre-tax income of $126,582). Assuming the corporation distributes exactly $100,000 as a dividend from pre-existing after-tax earnings: Shareholder pays qualified dividend tax: $100,000 × 20% = $20,000 + 3.8% NIIT = $23,800 total. Corporate tax on the income that generated the dividend (if $100,000 pre-tax earnings): $21,000. Total tax on dividend: $21,000 + $23,800 = $44,800. Salary is generally more tax-efficient for owner-employees in the 37% bracket — the corporate deduction effectively reduces the income to zero at the entity level, and only individual tax (plus FICA) applies, avoiding the double-tax layer of dividends.
explanations.c: This answer correctly identifies the approximate tax amounts but reaches an incorrect conclusion — dividends ($41,000-$44,800 total) are not always more tax-efficient than salary ($52,000-$56,000 total) at the 37%/20% brackets because FICA significantly increases the cost of salary. However, for owner-employees near or above the Social Security wage base ($168,600 in 2024), additional salary above that amount avoids the full FICA hit, potentially making salary competitive with dividends.
explanations.d: Whether salary or dividends produce lower total tax depends on the specific income amounts and rate brackets. For owner-employees earning above the SS wage base, additional salary incurs only 2.9% Medicare FICA vs. the 21% corporate + 23.8% effective dividend rate. The comparison requires specific calculation and is not categorical.

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: C corporation shareholder planning — proposed transaction implications for both entity and shareholder (noncash contributions and distributions)
questions.text: A C corporation shareholder plans to sell appreciated stock (basis $80,000, FMV $320,000) to the corporation itself (a stock redemption). The shareholder owns 100% of the corporation before the redemption and will own 0% after. What is the tax treatment of the $320,000 received by the shareholder?

answers.text: The $320,000 is treated as a dividend — all redemptions from closely held corporations where the shareholder is the sole owner are taxable as ordinary dividends
The $320,000 is tax-free because the shareholder is simply recovering their investment in the corporation through the redemption

The $320,000 is treated as proceeds from the sale or exchange of stock — capital gain of $240,000 ($320,000 − $80,000 basis), eligible for long-term capital gain rates if the stock is held more than one year
The $320,000 is treated as ordinary income equal to the full redemption price because the corporation deducts redemptions as compensation to shareholder-employees

explanations.a: Complete termination of a shareholder's interest qualifies as a sale or exchange treatment (not dividend) under §302(b)(3). Complete termination — reducing ownership from 100% to 0% — is one of the three tests under §302 that qualifies a redemption for sale or exchange treatment rather than dividend treatment.
explanations.b: The shareholder is not simply recovering their $80,000 basis tax-free — the entire amount up to basis is tax-free, but the $240,000 excess represents realized gain that is taxable (as capital gain under sale or exchange treatment).
explanations.c: Under §302(b)(3), a redemption that completely terminates a shareholder's entire interest in the corporation is treated as a sale or exchange: (1) The shareholder had 100% ownership and is reduced to 0% — this is a complete termination qualifying under §302(b)(3); (2) Tax treatment: the $320,000 received is treated as proceeds from the sale of stock; (3) Gain = $320,000 − $80,000 basis = $240,000 capital gain; (4) If the stock was held more than one year, the $240,000 is long-term capital gain taxed at preferential rates (0/15/20% + 3.8% NIIT); (5) This is significantly more favorable than dividend treatment (at ordinary income rates up to 37%) and is a primary reason shareholders structure complete exits through redemptions that qualify under §302(b)(3) rather than partial redemptions that might be recharacterized as dividends.
explanations.d: Stock redemptions are not deductible by the corporation as compensation. The corporation uses after-tax funds (or borrowed funds) to purchase the stock — the redemption payment is not a deductible compensation expense. This is a fundamental difference between salary/bonus (deductible) and stock redemption (non-deductible).

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: C corporation shareholder planning — proposed transaction implications for both entity and shareholder (noncash contributions and distributions)
questions.text: A C corporation plans to distribute its appreciated office building (basis $200,000, FMV $800,000) to its sole shareholder. The shareholder's stock basis is $150,000 and the corporation has $600,000 of accumulated E&P. Analyze the total tax consequences to both the corporation and the shareholder from this nonliquidating property distribution.

answers.text: Corporation: no gain recognized; Shareholder: $800,000 dividend income taxed at qualified dividend rates; total tax = $800,000 × 23.8% (20% + 3.8% NIIT)

Corporation: recognizes $600,000 gain ($800,000 FMV − $200,000 basis) taxed at 21%; Shareholder: receives $800,000 FMV distribution treated as $600,000 dividend (from E&P) plus $200,000 return of basis; shareholder's stock basis is reduced to $0 by the basis return
Corporation: no gain recognized on property distribution to a sole shareholder; Shareholder: $600,000 gain (FMV $800,000 minus basis $200,000) passes through to shareholder

Corporation: recognizes $600,000 gain taxed at 21% = $126,000 corporate tax; E&P increases by $600,000 gain then decreases by $800,000 FMV distribution; net E&P after = $600,000 + $600,000 − $800,000 = $400,000; Shareholder: $800,000 FMV of distribution = dividend to extent of E&P; since accumulated E&P ($600,000) + current E&P increase ($600,000 gain recognized) = $1,200,000 > $800,000 distribution, the entire $800,000 is a dividend at qualified dividend rates; shareholder stock basis unchanged (full distribution was dividend)

explanations.a: Under §311(b), the corporation DOES recognize gain when it distributes appreciated property in a nonliquidating distribution. The gain is $600,000 ($800,000 FMV − $200,000 basis). Option A incorrectly states the corporation recognizes no gain.
explanations.b: This answer correctly identifies the §311(b) corporate gain but miscalculates the E&P balance. The E&P increases by the $600,000 recognized gain before the distribution reduces it — the shareholder's dividend is determined by total E&P after the gain recognition, which may change the amount treated as dividend vs. return of basis.
explanations.c: §311(b) requires corporations to recognize gain on distributions of appreciated property — the 'no gain recognition' treatment applies only to individuals and partnerships. The pass-through characterization in option D is incorrect for C corporations.
explanations.d: Complete analysis: (1) Corporation-level: §311(b) gain = $800,000 FMV − $200,000 basis = $600,000. Corporate tax = $600,000 × 21% = $126,000. E&P computation: Accumulated E&P before distribution = $600,000. Add: §311(b) gain recognized = $600,000. E&P before distribution = $1,200,000. Distribution reduces E&P by FMV = $800,000. Ending E&P = $400,000. (2) Shareholder-level: Distribution amount = $800,000 (FMV of property per §301(b)). Taxed as dividend to extent of E&P = min($800,000, $1,200,000 E&P) = $800,000 dividend. Shareholder recognizes $800,000 of qualified dividend income. Shareholder's basis in the building = $800,000 FMV (§301(d)). The shareholder's stock basis ($150,000) is NOT reduced because the entire $800,000 was absorbed by E&P as a dividend — return of basis and capital gain only occur after E&P is exhausted.

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: S corporation planning — BIG tax, termination of S election, proposed transactions (contributions, distributions, loans, AEP vs. AAA elections)
questions.text: A former C corporation converted to S corporation status 3 years ago. At the time of conversion, the corporation had a building with a fair market value of $500,000 and an adjusted basis of $150,000. The S corporation now plans to sell the building for $520,000. Which tax applies to this sale?

answers.text: The built-in gains tax under §1374 applies to the $350,000 of net unrealized built-in gain at the time of the S election ($500,000 FMV − $150,000 basis), with the tax computed at the highest corporate rate (21%)
No special tax applies — S corporations are pass-through entities, and gain on asset sales passes through to shareholders without entity-level tax
The built-in gains tax applies only to the $20,000 of gain recognized after the S election ($520,000 sale price − $500,000 FMV at conversion)
The entire $370,000 of gain ($520,000 − $150,000) is subject to the corporate alternative minimum tax at the time of the S election

explanations.a: Built-in gains tax analysis: (1) Net unrealized built-in gain (NUBIG) at conversion = $500,000 FMV − $150,000 basis = $350,000 (this is the 'recognized built-in gain' subject to §1374); (2) Recognition period: the BIG tax applies to gains recognized within 5 years of the S election — the sale occurs in year 3, which is within the 5-year window; (3) BIG tax = $350,000 recognized built-in gain × 21% (highest corporate rate) = $73,500 entity-level tax; (4) The $20,000 of post-conversion appreciation ($520,000 − $500,000 FMV at conversion) is NOT subject to BIG tax — only the pre-conversion built-in gain is taxed at the entity level; (5) The $20,000 passes through to shareholders as regular S corporation income; (6) The BIG tax paid by the S corporation is generally deductible by the S corporation, reducing the pass-through to shareholders.
explanations.b: The built-in gains (BIG) tax under §1374 is specifically designed to prevent C corporations from converting to S status to avoid entity-level tax on appreciated assets. The BIG tax imposes a corporate-level tax on recognized built-in gains during the 5-year recognition period following the S election.
explanations.c: Only the $350,000 of built-in gain (pre-conversion appreciation) is subject to the BIG tax — not the post-conversion $20,000 gain. The §1374 tax is specifically targeted at gains that accrued during the C corporation years.
explanations.d: The corporate AMT was repealed for most purposes under TCJA. More fundamentally, the §1374 built-in gains tax is a separate provision from the AMT. The BIG tax applies to post-conversion dispositions of assets that were appreciated at the conversion date, computed at the regular 21% rate — not an alternative minimum tax.

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: S corporation planning — BIG tax, termination of S election, proposed transactions (contributions, distributions, loans, AEP vs. AAA elections)
questions.text: An S corporation has an Accumulated Adjustments Account (AAA) of $80,000, accumulated earnings and profits (AEP) from prior C corporation years of $60,000, and a shareholder with stock basis of $120,000. The shareholders want to distribute $100,000 this year. Management is considering whether to make an election to treat distributions as coming from AEP first rather than AAA. Compare the tax outcomes under each approach.

answers.text: AAA first (default): $80,000 from AAA (tax-free basis reduction) then $20,000 from AEP (dividend); AEP-first election: $60,000 from AEP (dividend) then $40,000 from AAA (tax-free basis reduction); AEP-first increases dividends by $40,000 and reduces tax-free distributions — the election is disadvantageous for shareholders in higher brackets

AAA first (default): $80,000 from AAA reduces basis to $40,000, $20,000 from AEP = $20,000 dividend income; AEP-first election: $60,000 from AEP = $60,000 dividend, $40,000 from AAA reduces basis from $120,000 to $80,000; under default, shareholders receive only $20,000 of dividends vs. $60,000 under election — default is more favorable for shareholders preferring basis reduction over dividend recognition
The election is tax-neutral — both approaches result in the same total taxes paid because total distributions are equal
The AEP-first election always reduces total taxes paid because accumulated E&P carries higher tax basis than AAA distributions

explanations.a: This correctly identifies which pool is tapped under each approach and correctly notes that the election increases dividends — but the framing is awkward. Option C presents the same analysis more clearly.
explanations.b: Distribution ordering analysis: Default (AAA first): (1) First $80,000 from AAA: reduces shareholder basis from $120,000 to $40,000; not currently taxable (previously taxed S income returned); (2) Next $20,000 from AEP: taxable dividend income ($20,000 × preferred dividend rate); remaining AEP = $60,000 − $20,000 = $40,000. AEP-first election (§1368(e)(3)): (1) First $60,000 from AEP: taxable dividend income ($60,000 × preferred dividend rate); remaining AEP = $0; (2) Next $40,000 from AAA: reduces basis from $120,000 to $80,000; not taxable. Comparison: Default produces $20,000 dividend; election produces $60,000 dividend. Shareholders prefer the default (less dividend income, more tax-free basis reduction). Why would anyone elect AEP-first? To accelerate elimination of AEP — once AEP is eliminated, there is no risk of dividend treatment on future distributions. This can be beneficial when the corporation plans large future distributions that might exceed AAA, or to simplify future distribution tracking.
explanations.c: The election is NOT tax-neutral — the total tax depends on the character of distributions. AAA distributions (return of previously taxed S income) are not taxable when within basis. AEP distributions are taxed as qualified dividends. The amounts taxed as dividends differ significantly between the two approaches ($20,000 vs. $60,000).
explanations.d: There is no general tax advantage to the AEP-first election for shareholders in high dividend-rate brackets. The election increases dividend income, which is taxable (even if at favorable qualified dividend rates), compared to AAA distributions that may be entirely tax-free basis reductions.

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: S corporation planning — BIG tax, termination of S election, proposed transactions (contributions, distributions, loans, AEP vs. AAA elections)
questions.text: An S corporation is planning to terminate its S election by issuing preferred stock to a new investor. A tax advisor warns that termination of the S election has significant consequences. Which statement BEST describes the tax effects of an S corporation terminating its S election?

answers.text: S election termination has no tax consequences — the corporation continues as a pass-through entity regardless of which election is in effect
S election termination requires full liquidation of the corporation — the corporation cannot continue operating as a C corporation after losing S status

Upon termination, the corporation immediately becomes a C corporation; a termination year is split into an S short year and a C short year for income allocation purposes; accumulated AAA becomes a post-termination transition period account available for tax-free shareholder distributions during the transition period
Upon termination, all accumulated AAA balances are immediately distributed to shareholders as taxable dividends because the corporation loses its S status

explanations.a: Terminating an S election converts the entity to a C corporation — a fundamentally different tax regime. The corporation is no longer a pass-through; income is taxed at the entity level at 21%, and distributions are dividends (not tax-free returns of basis). This has major tax consequences.
explanations.b: S corporations can and regularly do convert to C corporation status without liquidation — they simply continue operating under the new C corporation tax rules. Liquidation is not a requirement of S election termination.
explanations.c: S election termination mechanics: (1) Effective date: the termination is effective on the date the disqualifying event occurs (issuing preferred stock creates a second class of stock violating §1361(b)(1)(D)); (2) Split-year allocation: the tax year is divided into an S short year (beginning of year to termination date) and a C short year (termination date to year end); income is allocated between the two periods pro-rata (or via interim closing of books with shareholder consent); (3) Post-termination transition period (PTTP): for one year after the last day of the S corporation's last tax year, the corporation's AAA balance can be distributed tax-free to shareholders (reducing their stock basis) — this prevents AAA from becoming trapped in the now-C corporation where distributions would be dividends; (4) New C election is not re-electable: the corporation generally cannot re-elect S status for 5 years after termination without IRS consent.
explanations.d: The AAA is not immediately distributed as dividends upon termination. The post-termination transition period specifically protects AAA for one year of continued tax-free distributions to shareholders — preventing forced dividend treatment. This is a key taxpayer protection in the S election termination rules.

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: S corporation planning — BIG tax, termination of S election, proposed transactions (contributions, distributions, loans, AEP vs. AAA elections)
questions.text: Five years ago, a C corporation with $1,200,000 of appreciated assets (basis $300,000, FMV $1,200,000) elected S corporation status. It is now planning to sell all assets and liquidate. No assets have been sold during the S period, and asset values have increased to $1,500,000. The highest corporate rate is 21% and the shareholders' long-term capital gain rate is 20%. Analyze the built-in gains tax exposure and the total tax on the asset sale proceeds.

answers.text: BIG tax applies to the $900,000 of built-in gain ($1,200,000 FMV at election − $300,000 basis) at 21% = $189,000; shareholder capital gain tax on the remaining $300,000 of post-conversion appreciation at 20% = $60,000; plus shareholder-level tax on the net liquidation proceeds
BIG tax of $189,000 applies to the $900,000 pre-conversion built-in gain; after BIG tax, shareholders recognize the remaining proceeds as capital gain; total effective tax rate exceeds 40%
BIG tax applies to the full $1,200,000 of current gain ($1,500,000 − $300,000) at 21% because the 5-year recognition period only applies to former C corporations converted after 2012
No built-in gains tax — the 5-year recognition period has expired, so all gain is taxed only at the shareholder level at capital gain rates

explanations.a: Same issue as option B — BIG tax would apply only within the 5-year recognition period. Since the sale is in Year 6 (post-period), BIG tax does not apply to any of the gain, including the pre-conversion built-in gain.
explanations.b: While option B correctly identifies the BIG tax amount IF it applied, the 5-year recognition period has expired by Year 6, making BIG tax inapplicable. The analysis should begin with confirming whether the recognition period has passed.
explanations.c: The 5-year recognition period applies to all C-to-S conversions — it is not limited to corporations that converted after 2012. The period has been set at 5 years since 2012 (previous law had varying periods of 7 and 10 years). This option mischaracterizes the law and incorrectly applies BIG tax post-period.
explanations.d: Built-in gains tax recognition period analysis: The S corporation elected in Year 1 and is selling assets in Year 6. The 5-year recognition period (under current law following TCJA, which made the 5-year period permanent) runs from the date of S election through 5 full years. Year 6 is AFTER the 5-year recognition period has expired. Therefore: NO built-in gains tax applies to the Year 6 sale — §1374 BIG tax is only triggered for dispositions within the 5-year recognition period. The entire $1,200,000 gain ($1,500,000 − $300,000 basis) passes through to shareholders as S corporation income taxed at individual capital gain rates (assuming capital assets held long-term). Total shareholder tax = $1,200,000 × 20% (approximate) = $240,000. This is significantly better than if the sale occurred in Year 4 (within the BIG period), where $900,000 × 21% = $189,000 BIG tax would apply in addition to shareholder-level taxes. The 5-year waiting period is a primary planning consideration for C-to-S conversions — corporations with appreciated assets often wait the full 5 years before selling.

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: Partnership tax planning — contribution and distribution planning, guaranteed payments, proposed transaction implications for partner and partnership
questions.text: A partner receives a $30,000 guaranteed payment from a partnership for services rendered. The partnership's total ordinary income (before the guaranteed payment deduction) is $120,000. How is the $30,000 guaranteed payment treated for federal income tax purposes?

answers.text: The guaranteed payment is treated as ordinary income to the receiving partner and is deductible by the partnership (reducing partnership income allocated to all partners)
The guaranteed payment is tax-free to the partner because it is a return of the partner's capital investment in the partnership
The guaranteed payment is treated as a dividend from the partnership and is taxed at qualified dividend rates to the partner
The guaranteed payment is treated as a draw against the partner's capital account and has no income tax consequences until the partnership is liquidated

explanations.a: Under IRC §707(c), guaranteed payments are treated as payments to a non-partner for purposes of tax characterization: (1) To the receiving partner: the guaranteed payment is ordinary income, includible in the partner's gross income for the tax year the partnership has a tax year ending. The payment is not subject to self-employment tax limitations that apply to general partner distributive shares (though guaranteed payments for services are generally subject to self-employment tax); (2) To the partnership: the guaranteed payment is deductible as a business expense (reducing ordinary income allocated to all partners, including the recipient partner's distributive share of the reduced income). Partnership income after guaranteed payment = $120,000 − $30,000 = $90,000 allocated to all partners per their profit ratios. The recipient partner has $30,000 guaranteed payment income PLUS their share of the $90,000 reduced partnership income.
explanations.b: Guaranteed payments are not a return of capital — they are compensation to the partner for services or capital provided, regardless of partnership income or loss. Return of capital describes basis-reducing distributions, not service compensation.
explanations.c: Partnerships are not corporations and do not pay 'dividends.' Partnership income flows through as ordinary income, capital gain, or other specifically characterized items — not dividends. Guaranteed payments are specifically characterized as ordinary income under §707(c).
explanations.d: A draw against a capital account is a distribution of previously contributed capital or accumulated partnership profits — it is not guaranteed payment treatment. Guaranteed payments are current-year income regardless of the partner's capital account balance.

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: Partnership tax planning — contribution and distribution planning, guaranteed payments, proposed transaction implications for partner and partnership
questions.text: A partner with a 40% profit and loss interest and outside basis of $50,000 contributes property (basis $80,000, FMV $130,000) to the partnership and receives a $30,000 cash distribution simultaneously. Analyze the tax consequences of this transaction.

answers.text: No gain recognized; partner's new outside basis = $80,000 (carryover from contributed property); the distribution reduces basis to $50,000
No gain is recognized; outside basis after contribution = $50,000 + $80,000 (contributed property basis) − $30,000 (cash received treated as boot/distribution) = $100,000
The partner recognizes $30,000 of ordinary income because the distribution is treated as a guaranteed payment for the property contribution
The partner recognizes gain of $30,000 — the cash received in excess of the partner's share of partnership liabilities is boot; gain = cash received ($30,000)

explanations.a: Option A incorrectly computes the new outside basis. The partner's pre-contribution outside basis ($50,000) must be added to the contributed property basis ($80,000), and the cash distribution reduces the result. The new outside basis = $50,000 + $80,000 − $30,000 = $100,000, not $50,000.
explanations.b: Transaction analysis — contribution plus distribution: (1) §721 nonrecognition: no gain or loss on the property contribution ($80,000 basis property for partnership interest); (2) Partner's outside basis after contribution: pre-contribution basis $50,000 + contributed property basis $80,000 = $130,000 (before distribution); (3) Cash distribution under §731: $30,000 cash distribution; reduces outside basis = $130,000 − $30,000 = $100,000; no gain recognized because cash ($30,000) < outside basis ($130,000); (4) If the distribution is viewed as part of the same transaction as the contribution, the analysis is the same — aggregate outside basis = $50,000 + $80,000 − $30,000 = $100,000; no gain because pre-contribution outside basis ($50,000) is not exceeded by the cash distribution. The partnership's inside basis in the contributed property = $80,000 (§723 carryover).
explanations.c: A simultaneous cash distribution with a property contribution is not characterized as a guaranteed payment. This is a contribution and distribution — the §721 nonrecognition rules apply to the contribution, and the §731 distribution rules apply to the cash.
explanations.d: Boot triggering gain recognition applies to §351 (C corporation) contributions when boot is received. In a partnership §721 contribution, the general rule is no gain recognition. Cash distributions from partnerships reduce outside basis and trigger gain only if cash exceeds outside basis — here, $30,000 cash is less than the total outside basis ($130,000 after the contribution), so no gain.

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: Partnership tax planning — contribution and distribution planning, guaranteed payments, proposed transaction implications for partner and partnership
questions.text: A limited partnership is planning to sell investment real estate (basis $400,000, FMV $900,000) that was contributed by one partner three years ago (the contributing partner's original basis was $400,000 and FMV at contribution was $700,000). The partnership has three equal partners. How should the $500,000 total gain be allocated?

answers.text: $500,000 allocated equally — $166,667 per partner — because all three are equal partners

$300,000 allocated to the contributing partner (built-in gain at contribution: $700,000 − $400,000) and $200,000 allocated equally ($66,667 each) to all three partners as post-contribution appreciation

$300,000 allocated to the contributing partner (§704(c) built-in gain) and the remaining $200,000 allocated equally: $66,667 to each of the three partners (including the contributing partner receiving an additional $66,667)
$500,000 allocated entirely to the contributing partner because §704(c) requires all gain from contributed property to go to the contributing partner

explanations.a: Section 704(c) prevents the equal allocation approach for built-in gain property. The built-in appreciation at contribution ($300,000) must be specially allocated to the contributing partner — not shared equally.
explanations.b: Option B correctly identifies the §704(c) built-in gain ($300,000 to contributing partner) but incorrectly states that the remaining $200,000 is allocated 'equally to all three.' All three partners share the $200,000, but 'equally' means each gets $66,667 — so the contributing partner also receives their one-third share of post-contribution appreciation.
explanations.c: Correct §704(c) allocation: (1) Built-in gain at contribution = $700,000 FMV − $400,000 basis = $300,000 — allocated entirely to the contributing partner; (2) Post-contribution appreciation = $900,000 sale price − $700,000 FMV at contribution = $200,000 — allocated equally: $66,667 per partner (including the contributing partner receiving their 1/3 share); (3) Total gain allocation: Contributing partner: $300,000 + $66,667 = $366,667; Partner 2: $66,667; Partner 3: $66,667; Total: $500,000. The contributing partner bears all the pre-contribution built-in gain plus their pro-rata share of post-contribution appreciation — consistent with the economic reality that the contributing partner was the economic owner of the built-in appreciation at the time of contribution.
explanations.d: Section 704(c) allocates only the BUILT-IN GAIN at contribution to the contributing partner — not all future gains. Post-contribution appreciation ($200,000) is shared by all partners according to their profit-sharing ratios.

questions.name: Entity Tax Planning
questions.keyword: Partnership tax planning — contribution and distribution planning, guaranteed payments, proposed transaction implications for partner and partnership
questions.text: Two partners are considering the tax implications of dissolving their equal partnership. Partner A has an outside basis of $200,000; Partner B has an outside basis of $80,000. The partnership has: cash $100,000; land (basis $60,000, FMV $180,000); equipment (basis $40,000, FMV $70,000). Plan A: distribute all assets in-kind. Plan B: sell all assets and distribute cash. Compare the total tax consequences under each plan assuming the partners pay 20% capital gain tax on long-term gains.

answers.text: Plan A and Plan B produce identical tax outcomes because partnerships are pass-through entities where total tax is determined only by the gain amount, not timing
Plan B produces lower total tax because selling assets at the partnership level allows the §1231 netting rules to reduce overall gain recognition
Plan A is always preferable because in-kind distributions permanently eliminate tax on built-in gains of partnership assets

Plan A (in-kind): no gain at distribution (§731); each partner receives substituted basis in assets; tax deferred until later sale of received assets; Plan B (sell first): partnership recognizes $150,000 total gain (land $120,000 + equipment $30,000); gain allocated 50/50; each partner pays capital gain tax on $75,000 = $15,000 each ($30,000 total); current tax = $30,000 vs. Plan A deferral

explanations.a: While the total gain amount is the same in both plans, the TIMING of tax recognition differs significantly. Plan A defers tax until the distributee partners sell the received assets; Plan B creates current tax liability. The time value of money makes these economically different.
explanations.b: §1231 netting occurs at the partner level when they sell their distributed assets in Plan A — the netting rules apply in either scenario. Selling at the partnership level in Plan B may actually lose the ability for individual partners to net §1231 gains with their personal §1231 losses.
explanations.c: In-kind distributions defer but do not eliminate tax. The built-in gain is preserved in the distributee's lower substituted basis — when they later sell the assets, they recognize the gain. Only the §1202 QSBS exclusion or other specific provisions can permanently eliminate gain.
explanations.d: Comparison: Plan A (in-kind liquidating distribution): (1) §731: generally no gain/loss recognized at distribution of property only; (2) Each partner receives assets with substituted basis = remaining outside basis after cash; Partner A: receives half of each asset; Partner B: receives half; (3) Partner A's outside basis ($200,000) − cash ($50,000) = $150,000 basis allocated to received property; Partner B's outside basis ($80,000) − cash ($50,000) = $30,000 basis allocated to received property; (4) Future tax deferred until partners sell their portions of land and equipment. Plan B (sell assets, distribute cash): (1) Partnership sells: land gain = $180,000 − $60,000 = $120,000; equipment gain = $70,000 − $40,000 = $30,000; total gain = $150,000; (2) Each partner's 50% share = $75,000 gain; (3) Current tax: each partner pays $75,000 × 20% = $15,000; total current tax = $30,000; (4) After-tax cash distributed; (5) Planning consideration: Partner B with $80,000 outside basis and $30,000 received basis in the in-kind distribution would recognize substantial gain sooner on resale vs. Partner A who has higher basis. The choice between plans depends on partners' tax situations and plans for the received assets.
